narrative:
The model estimated a 56% chance you would fail the bar exam on the first attempt, meaning it judged failure slightly more likely than success. Because this crossed the decision threshold, your law school application was rejected. This is a probability, not a certainty: the same assessment implies a meaningful chance of passing.

The strongest factor pushing the prediction toward failure was your plan to study part-time. Among accepted students, nearly all study full-time, and part-time status is uncommon, so the model treated it as a risk signal. The second most influential factor was your undergraduate GPA of 2.40, well below the accepted-student average of about 3.23, which also pushed toward failure. The third factor, family income, worked in your favor: upper-middle income is common among accepted students, so it slightly pushed toward passing, though not enough to offset the first two factors. Other information was considered but had less influence.

To strengthen a future application, focus on what you can change. Demonstrate academic readiness through additional coursework or a post-baccalaureate record, prepare carefully to retake the LSAT, and consider a full-time study plan or a clear explanation of how you would manage part-time demands. You may also ask admissions whether conditional admission or feedback is available.
